set.body:
FOUND BY NEARLY FILING A FALSE BUG AGAINST IT. Recording the near-miss because the failure mode is a careful reader concluding the package is broken.

introduction.Rmd:296-300 states:

  'On the feature-additive metric path, including the current Euclidean default K = I,
   normalization = "conservative" makes each feature distribute unit mass across
   overlapping rows and local total geometry sums to global geometry.'

I tested that law directly. Conservative searchlights summed to 3.547005014; the global geometry read 0.4433756268. Ratio exactly 8.0, which is P, the feature count. My first reading was that the documented conservation law fails.

IT DOES NOT FAIL. The sentence omits a precondition: the GLOBAL side must also be summed rather than averaged. With normalization matched, the law holds exactly and more strongly than stated:

  whole_brain(none)                          3.547005014
  whole_brain(conservative)                  3.547005014
  whole_brain(local)                         0.4433756268     <- the default, and P times smaller
  voxels(none)                               3.547005014
  conservative searchlights, radius 1.01     3.547005014
  conservative searchlights, radius 2.01     3.547005014
  conservative searchlights, radius 3.01     3.547005014
  conservative searchlights, radius 99       3.547005014

  conservative local sum vs whole_brain(none): ratio 1, agreement to 1e-10

The total is INVARIANT TO THE SPATIAL FRAME under conservative normalization, across radii spanning the whole domain. That is a stronger and more attractive result than the sentence claims, and the vignette undersells it.

THE DEFECT IS THE MISSING PRECONDITION, and it is worse than an ordinary omission because of which default it collides with. whole_brain() defaults to local normalization, which is an AVERAGE. Conservative searchlights distribute unit MASS, which sums. So the reader who checks the documented law the most natural way - conservative searchlights against whole_brain() with defaults - gets a discrepancy of exactly P and no indication why. On a real brain P is tens of thousands, so the apparent violation is enormous.

This matters more here than in a package that made fewer promises. The conservation law is one of the framework's genuine selling points, it is the kind of claim a skeptical reader will want to verify before adopting, and verifying it the obvious way makes it look false.

FIX, cheap:
  1. state the precondition in the sentence: the comparison holds when the global frame is
     also mass-preserving, i.e. normalization 'none' or 'conservative', not the 'local' default
  2. state the stronger true claim - the conservative total is invariant to the frame, and
     equals the voxel-level and whole-brain totals
  3. show it in a runnable chunk. It is four lines, it is the most convincing evidence in the
     package that the unification claim has teeth, and it currently appears nowhere.

METHOD NOTE FOR THE RECORD: the tell that this was my error rather than the package's was the ratio being exactly P. Anyone testing these laws should check whether a discrepancy is a round factor of the feature count before filing.
set.title: The conservation law is stated without its precondition, so checking it the obvious way appears to fail by a factor of P
